excerpt: One folder tree you can build in ten minutes, how to put a file on the right shelf, and how to repair a heap of old files without reading every one.

body.text: This lesson gives you a folder structure for school or work that you can build in about ten minutes. You will make it, put three real files in it, and repair an old folder that has become a heap. If your Documents folder already feels like a bag of loose papers, this is the fix.
A structure is not a decoration. It is a promise that a file has one obvious place to live, so the next time you need it you look once instead of everywhere.
Before you start

items: A computer with Documents open.
Three real files you use often, such as a CV, a receipt, and a certificate.
Ten minutes, and no need to empty anything first.

body.text: Build the tree
Three levels are enough for a person. More than that and you begin hiding files from yourself, because you have to remember a path instead of a name.

items: Open Documents.
Make one folder called School or Work, whichever fits your week.
Inside it, make one folder per year: 2026, 2027.
Inside 2026, make folders for the things that repeat: Fees, Certificates, Forms.
Make one more top-level folder called Personal, and stop there.
Name nothing Misc or New folder, because neither tells you what is inside.

body.text: You will see the tree in the left column of File Explorer once the folders exist, with small arrows to open and close each level. That column is the map, and it stays visible while you work.

body.alt: File Explorer showing a tree of folders for school and personal files.
body.caption: Three levels: area, year, topic. The tree in the left column is the map you will use every day.

body.text: Put a file on the right shelf
A good name answers three questions without opening the file: what it is, who it belongs to, and when it was made. That is all a name needs to do.

items: Start with the subject: fees, cv, certificate, receipt.
Add the person or the place if the folder holds more than one person's files.
End with the date, written year first: 2026-10.
Use hyphens between words, not spaces, which some systems drop or double.
Save the file directly into the right folder the first time, rather than moving it later.

body.text: It looks like moving files around later is tidier. In practice a file moved three times is a file deleted twice, and the small effort at the moment of saving is what keeps the tree honest.
Do not worry if the first week is imperfect. A structure that is right within a month beats a perfect plan you never start.
Repair an old heap
Most people have a folder with two hundred files in it, all saved at the same level. You do not need to sort every one. Sort the ones you will need, and leave the rest until a rainy afternoon.

items: Open the heap and switch the view to Details.
Click the Date modified column so the newest files appear first.
Move the twenty newest files into the correct folders.
Create a folder called Archive 2025, and move everything older than this year into it.
Leave the Archive folder alone after that, and open it only when you need an old document.
Delete anything you can see you will never open again.

body.text: You will see the heap shrink as files move, and the folder count grow. Twenty moves is a visible change, and it is enough to make tomorrow easier.

body.alt: A desk with a notebook, a pen, and a laptop showing organised folders.
body.caption: Sort what you will use this month, archive the rest, and leave the archive closed. That is the whole repair.

body.text: If it goes wrong
None of these loses a file, because moving a file inside the same disk is reversible.

items: You moved a file and cannot find it: press Ctrl and Z, or search for its name.
A file will not move: it is open in another program. Close the program and try again.
Two folders have the same name: rename one with the year, such as Fees 2026.
You created too many folders: delete the empty ones. An empty folder is a sign of a plan that was too fine.
The tree looks wrong on a phone: cloud apps show folders differently. The structure still holds.
You accidentally deleted a folder: restore it from the Recycle Bin, which keeps whole folders.

body.text: Practice
Build it today with three files. The structure is only real once it holds something.

items: Build the area, year, and topic folders in Documents.
Save three real files into the right folders.
Rename one file so it follows the subject-date pattern.
Sort the newest ten files in your busiest folder.
Create an Archive folder and move last year's files into it.

body.text: You can now find any file in two clicks instead of ten minutes of searching. In the next lesson you will rename files without breaking the links between them.

excerpt: How to rename a file safely, why the extension matters, which characters break a file, and why the word final causes arguments in offices.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to rename a file without breaking it. You will learn the safe way to rename, which part of a name to leave alone, and how to name files so that a busy office can tell one version from another.

A file name has two parts. The name you choose comes first, and the extension comes after the dot, such as .docx or .pdf. The extension is what tells the computer which program opens the file, so it is the part to leave alone.
If you have renamed something and it stopped opening, you are not the first, and the fix takes one minute. The file itself is almost never damaged.
Before you start

items: One file you do not mind practising with.
File Explorer open on the folder that holds it.

body.text: The slow click and the F2 key
There are three ways to rename a file, and one of them is much safer than the others for a beginner.
Nothing you do here changes what is inside a document, so take your time and read the name before you press Enter.
You will see the name change in the list as soon as you press Enter, and the icon stay exactly the same.

items: Click the file once to select it, then press F2.
The name becomes editable with the extension left out, which is the safest version.
Type the new name and press Enter.
Or right-click the file and choose Rename.
Or click the name twice slowly, which is not the same as a double-click.

body.text: You will see the name highlighted in a box, ready for typing, with the extension sitting outside the highlight or left visible. If the whole name including .docx is highlighted, do not press Enter until you are sure you want to change the extension too.

body.alt: A file selected in a folder with its name in edit mode.
body.caption: F2 selects the name and leaves the extension alone. That is the safest way to rename a file.

body.text: A name that survives a busy office
The test of a name is whether a stranger can tell which file is newest without opening any of them. Most offices fail that test, and then argue about it.

items: Put the subject first: minutes, invoice, cv, report.
Put the date last, year first: 2026-10-29.
Add the person or department when more than one exists.
Use hyphens instead of spaces.
Keep it under about forty characters so it stays readable in a list.
Never use final, final2, latest, or new in a name.

body.text: It looks like final tells the reader something. It tells them nothing, because every earlier version was also final on the day it was saved. A date and a version number say the same thing honestly.

body.alt: A folder with files named by subject and date.
body.caption: Subject, person, date. A list sorted by name is then also sorted by time.

body.text: Characters that cause trouble
Most characters are fine in a name. A few are not, and they cause failures that look like corruption.

items: Do not use \ / : * ? " < > | in a name. Windows reserves them.
Avoid a full stop at the end of a name.
Avoid two different files called report and Report in the same folder, because some systems treat them as the same.
Avoid the ampersand and the naira sign if the file will be emailed, because older mail systems misread them.
Do not rename a file that is being uploaded or synced, because the sync can cancel.

body.text: If a name is refused, the message usually says which character is the problem. Read it rather than retyping the whole name, and the fix takes five seconds.
If it goes wrong
Renaming does not touch what is inside the file, so even a bad rename is easy to undo.
None of these loses the file, so read them without alarm and try the first fix.

items: The file will not open after renaming: you removed or changed the extension. Rename it back, or add the original ending.
You cannot see the extension to restore it: open the View menu and tick File name extensions.
Two files will not sit in the same folder: the names are identical. Add a date to one.
The file turned into a white blank icon: the program that opens it is missing, and the file is intact. Open it with the right program.
You renamed the wrong file: press Ctrl and Z, which undoes the rename.
A shared file has two versions with the same name: keep the newer one, rename the older with the word archive and its date.

body.text: Practice
Rename three files today, and the pattern will stick.

items: Rename one file with F2, and leave the extension alone.
Rename a second file to the subject-person-date pattern.
Deliberately change an extension to see what the warning looks like, then change it back.
Turn on file name extensions in the View menu.
Find one file called final or new in your folders and give it a real name.

body.text: You can now name a file so that the person receiving it knows what it is and when it was made. In the next lesson you will find a file whose name you have forgotten.

excerpt: How to search for a file when you remember only half the name, where to search first, and what to do when the search box finds nothing at all.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to find a file you have lost. You will search by half a name, by the day you remember, and by what is inside the document. You will also learn why a search sometimes finds nothing, and what to do next.
Search looks at file names and, on most machines, at the words inside files. It is fast, but it can only find what exists. A file that was never saved is not hiding, and no search will produce it.
Before you start

items: The computer you saved the file on. A different machine cannot see it.
One detail you remember: a word, a date, or a person's name.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Stand in the right room first
The search box at the top of File Explorer searches the folder you are standing in, and everything below it. Searching from Documents will not find a file sitting on the Desktop.

items: Open File Explorer and click This PC to search every drive at once.
Type part of the name in the search box at the top right.
Press Enter and wait, even if nothing appears at first.
Switch the view to Details and sort by Date modified if you remember when you last used it.
Double-click a result to open it, and note the folder shown in the address bar.

body.text: You will see results appear while you type, and the word search appears in the address bar with a small X to clear it. Search runs in the background, so a slow old machine may take ten seconds to fill the list.

body.alt: File Explorer with a search term typed in the search box.
body.caption: Search from This PC to cover every drive. Search from Documents and you only search Documents.

body.text: Half a name, and the day you remember
You rarely remember a full name. Search is forgiving about that, and there are three tricks worth knowing.

items: Type one distinctive word, such as receipt, rather than the whole name you half remember.
Use an asterisk for the part you have forgotten: fee*2026 finds fee-slip-2026 and fees-2026.
Type a date in the form 2026-10 to find files with that in the name.
Search for a word you know is inside the document, which finds files with a different name.
Use ext: to search by type, such as ext:pdf to show only PDFs.
Sort by Date modified when the name is hopeless but the day is clear.

body.text: It looks like search covers the whole computer when you type in any box. It covers the folder you are in and everything under it, which is why the first result often depends on where you started.

body.alt: A person searching on a laptop at a desk with a notebook beside it.
body.caption: One distinctive word and a date beats a long guess. Search does not need the whole name.

body.text: When search finds nothing
A search that returns nothing is information, not failure. It tells you the file is not where you are looking, or not named what you think.

items: Search from This PC rather than a single folder.
Check Downloads, which quietly collects most of what the internet sends.
Open the Recycle Bin and restore the file if it is there.
Open the program and look at its recent files, which ignores names altogether.
Check the desktop and the flash drive that may still be plugged in.
Search a second device, because the file may have been saved on a phone.

body.text: Do not worry if the first search is empty. Most lost files are found on the third attempt, in a place the person had forgotten they used.
Make the next search short
Search is a repair. The habit that prevents the problem is naming files with the subject and the date, which is the previous lesson in this chapter.

items: Name files with the subject and the month, not with the date you felt like saving.
Keep one folder per area of your life, so there are fewer places to look.
Empty Downloads into the right folder once a week.
Back up the folders you would hate to search for again.

body.text: If it goes wrong
None of these is a dead end, and the last one explains most empty searches.

items: Search is very slow: close other programs, and search one drive at a time.
Search finds files but not the one you want: the name is different from what you remember. Search for a word inside it instead.
The search box is missing: you are in a view that hides it. Switch to Details view.
A file you can see is not found: the search index is out of date. Search from This PC and wait, or rebuild the index in Settings.
The file was never saved: no search can find it, and only the program's recovery or a backup will help.
You deleted it without using the bin: stop using the machine and ask a repairer about recovery before installing anything.

body.text: Practice
Ten minutes of searching your own machine teaches more than a page about it.

items: Search This PC for one word you know is in a file name.
Search using an asterisk in the middle of the word.
Search with ext:pdf and count how many PDFs you own.
Sort a folder by Date modified and find the oldest file.
Find one file in Downloads and move it to the right folder.

body.text: You can now find a file when the name has gone from your memory. In the next lesson you will meet the bar at the bottom of the screen and learn what every part of it does.

excerpt: What the Start menu is for, what the taskbar shows you, how to find a program you cannot see, and what to do when the taskbar disappears.

body.text: This lesson explains the Start menu and the taskbar, which together are the map of a Windows computer. You will find any program, see what is already running, and get the taskbar back when it hides. If a program seems to have vanished, this is where it went.

The taskbar is the strip along the bottom of the screen. The Start menu opens from the button at the left of it. Everything you do happens somewhere on that strip, even when the window in front of you is hiding it.
It is normal for a beginner to lose a window on the first day. The taskbar keeps every open program in one place, so nothing is ever really gone.
The Start button is a search box
You do not need to memorise where programs live. Type the first three letters of the name and press Enter.

items: Press the Windows key, or click the Start button.
Type the program's name, such as calc for Calculator.
The best match appears at the top with a highlighted row.
Press Enter to open it.
To keep it, right-click the result and choose Pin to taskbar.

body.text: You will see a list of matches change as you type, and a panel on the right with recently used files. If the list is empty for a second, the machine is still thinking, and the answer usually arrives before you finish typing.

body.alt: A Windows Start menu open with the search box in use.
body.caption: Type three letters and press Enter. The search box knows every program on the machine.

body.text: The taskbar tells you what is running
Every open window has an icon on the taskbar. A small line or a coloured background under the icon means that program is open. Clicking the icon brings it to the front.

items: A plain icon means the program is pinned but not open.
An icon with a line under it is open, even if you cannot see the window.
Hover over the icon to see a small preview of the window.
Right-click the icon for a jump list of recent files or actions.
Drag icons along the taskbar to arrange them in the order you work.

body.text: It looks like a program has closed itself when the window disappears. It is usually minimised, and one click on its taskbar icon brings it back with all your work in it.

At the right end of the taskbar is the system tray, which shows the clock, the network icon, the volume icon, and the small arrows for hidden items. Those icons answer most beginner questions about sound and internet in one look.

body.alt: A Windows taskbar with pinned and open program icons.
body.caption: A line under an icon means the program is open. That is how a window reappears without being reopened.

body.text: When the taskbar disappears
A hidden taskbar is a setting, not a fault. On some machines it slides away when the mouse is not near it, and returns when you point at the bottom edge.

items: Move the pointer to the very bottom of the screen and wait a second.
Press the Windows key, which brings the Start menu and the taskbar back.
Open Settings, then Personalisation, then Taskbar, and turn off Automatically hide the taskbar.
If the whole screen looks unfamiliar, try Ctrl, Alt and Delete, then choose Task Manager.
Restart from the Start menu if the strip stays missing.

body.text: None of this loses your open work, and the second step solves it in most cases.
If it goes wrong
These are the five things people ask about most, and every one has a short fix.

items: A pinned icon does nothing when clicked: the program was uninstalled. Right-click it and unpin.
Windows key does not open Start: the keyboard may be locked with Fn, or the key is failing. Click the Start button instead.
The clock shows the wrong time: right-click it, choose Adjust date and time, and set the time zone.
Too many icons on the taskbar: unpin the ones you do not use, and keep under ten.
The taskbar moved to the side: drag it back, or unlock it in Settings and set the location.

body.text: Practice
Two minutes with the search box today saves a week of hunting through menus.

items: Open three programs using only the Start search box.
Pin one of them to the taskbar, and unpin a program you never use.
Open a window, minimise it, then bring it back from the taskbar.
Read the clock, network, and volume icons in the system tray.
Turn automatic hiding off if your taskbar keeps disappearing.

body.text: You can now find any program without remembering where it lives, and bring back a window that seems to have closed. In the next lesson you will learn why a desktop icon can stop working when you copy it to another machine.

excerpt: What a shortcut really is, why desktop icons stop working on another computer, how to make one on purpose, and how to tell a shortcut from the file itself.

body.text: This lesson explains shortcuts: what they are, how to make one, and why they stop working when they travel to another computer. If a desktop icon has ever refused to open, this lesson explains what happened without blaming the machine.
A shortcut is a small file that points at another file, the way a signpost points at a town. The sign is not the town. If the town moves, the sign still stands there pointing at nothing.
If you have ever sent somebody an icon that arrived as a white page, you did nothing wrong. You sent the signpost instead of the town, and this lesson shows the difference.
Before you start

items: A file or program you use often.
About five minutes.

body.text: Tell a shortcut from the file
Shortcuts are drawn with a small bent arrow in the corner of the icon, or a small chain link on newer versions of Windows. That mark is the whole difference.
You will see a small arrow in the bottom-left corner of the icon, or a chain link on newer versions of Windows, and that mark is the only warning you get.

items: Look at the corner of the icon for a small arrow.
Right-click the icon and choose Properties.
A shortcut shows a Target field naming the real file.
The real file shows a Location field instead, and its size in megabytes.
A shortcut is a few kilobytes at most, whatever the file it points at weighs.
On a Mac, an alias has a small arrow too, and the same rules apply.

body.text: You will see the Target box in the Properties window with a path in it, such as C:\Users\Ada\Documents\cv.pdf. That path is where the real file lives, and the signpost is only telling you the way.

body.alt: A desktop icon with a small shortcut arrow in the corner.
body.caption: The small arrow means the icon is a signpost. The file it points at lives somewhere else.

body.text: Make one on purpose
A shortcut on the desktop is useful for the three things you open every day. More than that and the desktop becomes a noticeboard nobody reads.

items: Find the real file in File Explorer.
Right-click it and choose Show more options if your Windows hides it.
Choose Send to, then Desktop (create shortcut).
On a Mac, right-click and choose Make Alias, then drag it where you want it.
Rename the shortcut so it reads clearly, such as Fees folder.
Delete shortcuts you no longer use, since they clutter the desktop for no benefit.

body.text: It looks like copying an icon to a flash drive copies the file. It copies the signpost, which arrives on the other machine pointing at a folder that does not exist there.
This is the most common version of the problem: somebody sends a shortcut to a colleague, and the colleague sees a white icon and a message saying the item cannot be found.

body.alt: A desktop with several shortcut icons arranged in rows.
body.caption: Three shortcuts, three daily tasks. A desktop with thirty icons is a drawer nobody sorts.

body.text: When a sign breaks
A shortcut breaks for one of three reasons: the real file moved, the real file was deleted, or the shortcut travelled to another computer.
None of these loses your work, because a shortcut holds none of it. The file itself is sitting where you left it.

items: Check the Target path in Properties and see whether that folder still exists.
Use search to find the file's new location.
Delete the dead shortcut and make a new one from the real file.
If the file was deleted, look in the Recycle Bin before anything else.
If you need to send a file to somebody, send the file, not the icon.

body.text: None of this means the original file is gone, and the last line in the list prevents most cases on the day it matters.
If it goes wrong
Shortcuts are the least dangerous thing on a computer, because they hold no work of their own.

items: A desktop icon shows a white page: the target is missing, or the program was uninstalled.
The shortcut opens the wrong file: the target path is out of date. Rebuild the shortcut from the right file.
A shortcut cannot be deleted: it may be a system icon. Right-click the desktop, choose Personalisation, then change the desktop icons.
You copied a shortcut instead of the file: go back and copy the real file from its folder.
The shortcut works on your machine but not on another: expected. Send the file itself.
You have thirty shortcuts and cannot see the desktop picture: select them and delete the ones you do not use.

body.text: Practice
Five minutes on this prevents a support call that takes an hour.

items: Make a shortcut to a folder you use daily.
Right-click it and read the Target path.
Move the real file to another folder and see what the shortcut does.
Rebuild the shortcut from the new location.
Delete one shortcut you have not used this month.

body.text: You can now tell a signpost from a file, and you will not lose an afternoon sending one instead of the other. In the next lesson the chapter turns to sound, starting with volume.
